title: Slow-Moving Hurricane Nolo Threatens Hawaii with Catastrophic Flooding
summary: Hurricane Nolo wasn't supposed to be a problem. Last week, forecasters declared the storm was dissipating (falling apart) and wouldn't need more updates. Then it regenerated — and took a sharp right turn straight toward Hawaii. Now the Big Island is under a hurricane watch, and forecasters are warning of "life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides." As of Friday afternoon, Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, making it a Category 2 storm. But its forward speed was only 5 mph — slower than a brisk walk. That's dangerous because slow storms can dump rain on one area for hours. Some parts of the Big Island could see more than 2 feet of rain, with 10 to 25 inches expected more widely. Maui is under a tropical storm watch and could get up to 10 inches. Nolo is expected to strengthen to a Category 4 with winds up to 140 mph over the next 72 hours, fed by warm ocean waters. It's the latest in a busy Pacific hurricane season fueled by a powerful El Niño. Hawaii has already endured four major disasters this year: a Kona low in March that caused the worst flooding in over two decades, a 6.0 magnitude earthquake in May, Hurricane Lala in August, and Hurricane Lowell earlier this month. Governor Josh Green said those disasters damaged or destroyed about 1,290 homes and recovery could cost roughly $1 billion. "The time to finish preparations for significant heavy rain and flooding impacts on the Big Island is now," the National Hurricane Center said. The storm's slow forward speed means it could linger near the islands, dumping rain for hours. Forecasters warn that the combination of heavy rain and steep terrain raises the risk of mudslides. Residents are urged to prepare now, as conditions are expected to worsen over the next 72 hours. With warm ocean waters feeding the storm, Nolo could grow even stronger before it reaches the islands. Officials are closely monitoring the situation and advising residents to stay informed and ready to act.
why_it_matters: Hawaii's back-to-back disasters show how climate extremes stack up: a state still repairing damage from a flood, an earthquake and two hurricanes has less money, fewer shelters and less energy to face the next storm. Slow-moving, rain-heavy hurricanes like Nolo are exactly the kind scientists expect more of in a warming Pacific, which means emergency planning is becoming a permanent part of island life.

questions.question: What is fueling this busy Pacific hurricane season?

background_read: Hawaii (a U.S. state made up of islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, roughly 2,000 miles from the mainland) sits near the edge of the hurricane zone, so direct hits are rare but close calls happen often.

Hurricane Iniki devastated Kauai in 1992, and in 2018 Hurricane Lane passed near the islands and dumped record-breaking rain on the Big Island — reminders of how much damage even a storm that misses can cause.

The National Hurricane Center (the part of the U.S. government's weather and ocean agency that tracks and forecasts storms) uses the Saffir-Simpson scale, which ranks hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5 based on wind speed.
El Niño (a natural warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean that happens every few years) shifts weather patterns worldwide and tends to produce more and stronger storms in the Pacific.
Josh Green (Hawaii's governor since 2022) has led the state's response to a string of disasters this year, and says recovery from the damage so far could cost roughly $1 billion.
Slow-moving storms are especially dangerous on islands, where steep mountains and few roads can turn heavy rain into flooding and mudslides that cut whole communities off from help.

perspectives.description: Forecasters detected the storm's sharp turn and officials pushed residents to prepare immediately, with the National Hurricane Center warning that 'the time to finish preparations ... is now.' Hawaii has also been through four disasters this year, so agencies know their emergency playbook and can move people and supplies quickly.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — a community already at its limit
perspectives.description: The Big Island is still recovering from a Kona low, an earthquake and two hurricanes, with about 1,290 homes damaged or destroyed and recovery costs near $1 billion. Forecasters first said the storm was dissipating, which may have left some residents unprepared, and slow storms mean days of rain, blocked roads and delayed rescues.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — a pattern, not a one-off
perspectives.description: Hawaii lies near the edge of the hurricane zone, so it usually escapes direct hits, but El Niño years bring warmer water and more Pacific storms. Slow forward speed, warm ocean water and steep island terrain are a well-known, dangerous combination that turns wind into a rainfall and mudslide problem.

Everything depends on how strong Nolo becomes, how long it lingers and precisely where it tracks. Emergency managers must weigh whether to open shelters and prepare evacuations while the storm is still strengthening, and this year's repeated disasters raise a bigger question: how much longer can the same island community keep absorbing these costs?
